label: confirmed
text: Several First Nations, including Tsartlip and the St’at’imc Chiefs Council, filed Federal Court applications for judicial review of the Pacific Link pipeline’s national‑interest designation, alleging inadequate consultation and insufficient information; the government says the designation follows the Building Canada Act. The filings bring the total number of lawsuits against the designation to ten.

sources.title: Tsartlip file legal challenge of federal decision on Pacific Link pipeline
sources.articleText:
The Tsartlip First Nation has filed a legal challenge to the federal government's decision to list the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline between Alberta to B.C.'s coast as a project of national interest, fast-tracking its review.
A statement from the First Nation, located on the Saanich Peninsula, says it has filed a Federal Court application for judicial review on the move, saying Ottawa has not "given sufficient information about the project and its potential impacts."
The St'at'imc Chiefs Council, representing nine nations along the proposed pipeline route in B.C.'s Interior and Fraser Valley, says it has also launched legal action asking the court to overturn the listing as a project of national interest.
The group says in a statement that approving the Pacific Link project without full assessment of risks to salmon and fishing rights, and without deep consultation to ensure the consent of all impacted nations, is unacceptable and unlawful.
The Tsartlip application asks the court to confirm the Canadian government must "meaningfully consult" the nation before deciding if the pipeline is in the national interest.
The pipeline was the first project to receive the designation under the Building Canada Act during an announcement by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith last month.
The proposal is for a new pipeline that largely follows the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline to an export terminal in Metro Vancouver with an estimated cost between $35.2 billion and $42.7 billion.
The designation means the project would be subject to a fast-tracked, streamlined regulatory process conducted by the federal major projects office, a move Tsartlip First Nation spokesman Adam Olsen calls "reckless."
"The national interest designation concerns a multibillion-dollar publicly funded project that is not expected to be completed until 2032," Olsen says in the statement. "Yet the consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months."
Olsen, who's a former B.C. Green legislator, says there is concern there may be more projects of national interest affecting First Nations, citing last week's announcement that the Port of Vancouver's Roberts Bank Terminal 2 expansion has also been added to that list.
"How this decision is made will shape every one that follows, for our people, for future generations and for every community, First Nations or otherwise, that could be next," Olsen says.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 2, 2026.

sources.title: Nine more First Nations file court challenges to Pacific Link pipeline - National Post
sources.articleText:
The nine applicants include First Nations located along the proposed pipeline and tanker shipping routes
OTTAWA — Nine more First Nations have a filed court challenges against the federal government’s decision to designate the West Coast pipeline a project of national interest under Bill C-5, the Building Canada Act.
First Nations argue cabinet did not discharge its duty to consult and provide adequate accommodation, before deciding to fast-track the Pacific Link pipeline on Oct. 1.
The nine applicants from B.C. also argue the federal government erred by failing to exercise its powers under the BCA consistently with the statutory imperatives arising from the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (UNDA), which was passed by Parliament in 2021.
“This project being pre-approved does not meet the standard not only of free, prior, and informed consent, but the minimum standard of consultation,” said Terry Teegee, regional chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, during a press conference in Richmond, B.C., on Monday.
“We are very concerned about not only this project but other projects, and other First Nations should all be concerned across this country,” he added.
The legal challenges were filed in Federal Court last week, bringing the total number of lawsuits against Pacific Link’s national interest designation to 10, after Cold Lake First Nation in Alberta was the first to file on Oct. 8.
The nine applicants include First Nations located along the proposed pipeline and tanker shipping routes, as well as those not geographically located close the pipeline, but argue their fishing rights and livelihood rely on Fraser River salmon.
The Pacific Pipeline is the first project to be designated as a project of national interest under the government’s new major projects legislation. The legislation allows Cabinet to give projects in the national interest a fast-tracked regulatory process.
The proposed route will run 1,200 kilometres from Bruderheim, Alta., to a proposed large-tanker port in Delta, B.C.
The newly formed Major Projects Office undertook consultations with over 130 Indigenous communities between July 3 to Sept. 18, before the designation was announced.
The MPO will begin its review of the project in early 2027, with public hearings held by the commission of the Canada Energy Regulator. The MPO is expected to finalize a conditions document by Sept. 1, 2027.
The applicants argue the consultation process was inadequate and took place during the busy summer months.
“We were reached out to be engaged in late July with the deadline, and my community, we had a wildfire right above our community where it was two, five kilometers away and the letters came in,” said St’át’imc Chiefs Council Chairperson Chief Justin Kane.
Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline has so far agreed to take a minority 10 per cent private stake in the development, the publicly owned Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission is also a proponent. The Trans Mountain Corporation is leading the project.
Indigenous communities have been offered a 10 per-cent ownership stake in the pipeline project. The pipeline, once completed, is expected to generate over $20 billion in GDP per year and $100 billion in government revenue by 2060.
Government officials have acknowledged and are prepared for potential court challenges. Last week, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said he is confident Bill C-5 is Charter compliant.
“We believe that we’ve met the constitutional obligations that we have to act within the spheres of authorities that we have, while respecting importantly the rights of First Nations communities and Indigenous rights holders more broadly,” said Fraser, before a caucus meeting on Oct. 28. “To the extent that there are concerns, my hope is that we can work through them through negotiation.”
Teegee said the prime minister should be held accountable for taking advantage of the uncertainty of a trade war with the U.S. to pass Bill C-5 and its successor, Bill C-39, which is currently being studied by a legislative committee.
“It’s a process that Prime Minister Carney should be called out for,” he said. “He is utilizing taking advantage of a crisis for a bill that they’ve always wanted to pass, it’s nothing new.”
Robert Banks Terminal 2, a proposed project in Delta, B.C., that would increase the Port of Vancouver’s container capacity by approximately 50 per cent, was also designated a project of national interest by the federal government last Friday.
Robert Banks is the endpoint of the proposed Pacific Link pipeline.
“I can only project that this is just going to heat up more and more and more as more massive projects are approved without proper consultation with First Nations people, as was the port and the pipeline, and without any recognition of the real needs of reconciliation, this is not ending today,” said Hugh Baker, a political executive at the First Nations Summit.

sources.title: First Nation takes Ottawa to court over B.C. pipeline, alleging failure to consult - CTV News
sources.articleText:
First Nation takes Ottawa to court over B.C. pipeline, alleging failure to consult
Map showing the proposed Pacific Link pipeline corridors, which would carry crude oil from Bruderheim, Alta., to a planned export terminal near Delta, B.C. The final route has not yet been determined. (Pacific Link)
A Vancouver Island First Nation is taking the federal government to court, alleging Ottawa failed to properly consult its members before declaring a proposed oil pipeline a project of national interest.
W̱JOȽEȽP (Tsartlip First Nation) filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Oct. 30, challenging the designation of the proposed Pacific Link pipeline under the Building Canada Act.
The application alleges the government rushed the consultation process, provided insufficient information about the project and failed to adequately consider its potential impacts on the First Nation’s treaty rights.
At the heart of the challenge are Tsartlip’s rights under the 1852 North Saanich Treaty, which protects its members traditional fishing rights.
The First Nation says the proposed pipeline’s marine shipping route would pass through traditional fishing waters and harvesting areas around the Fraser River Delta and Strait of Georgia.
According to the court filing, federal officials consulted with Tsartlip between July 2 and Sept. 18, 2026. During that time, the First Nation says it repeatedly requested more information but received only general details about the project.
It also alleges Ottawa provided insufficient funding and imposed timelines that did not account for the community’s capacity to participate, including cultural and fishing activities during the summer.
Tsartlip submitted its concerns on Sept. 18, warning that consultation had not been adequate. Less than two weeks later, on Oct. 1, the federal government designated the pipeline a project of national interest.
Trevor Mercredi, Grand Chief of Treaty 8 First Nations, third from right, listens as Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith make an announcement in Fort McMurray, Alta., on Thursday Oct 1, 2026. Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Greg Halinda
Chief Curtis Olsen (TELX̱ILEM) says the decision puts the First Nation’s responsibilities to protect its traditional waters and future generations at risk.
“In 1852, the Crown made a promise in the Douglas Treaty that our people could continue to live from these waters as we always have,” Olsen said in a media release.
The designation has significant implications for how the project moves forward.
Under the Building Canada Act, certain federal authorizations are deemed to have been made in favour of the project once it receives national interest status. The legislation also allows exemptions from requirements under several federal laws, including the Fisheries Act and Impact Assessment Act.
Tsartlip argues that effectively moves key regulatory decisions ahead before the project has been fully developed or its impacts properly assessed.
The First Nation is also asking the court to rule that Ottawa must consult with it and obtain its consent before making another decision about the pipeline’s national interest designation.
The legal challenge also invokes the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and Canada’s legislation implementing it.
“The consultation and decision-making process happened in less than three months. That’s not efficient, that’s reckless,” said Adam Olsen (SȾHENEP), Tsartlip’s director of intergovernmental relations in a release.
The proposed Pacific Link pipeline would transport approximately one million barrels of crude oil per day from Bruderheim, Alta., to a new export terminal and offshore loading facility near Delta, B.C. The proposed route would stretch approximately 1,200 to 1,250 kilometres.
Map showing the proposed Pacific Link pipeline corridors, which would carry crude oil from Bruderheim, Alta., to a planned export terminal near Delta, B.C. The final route has not yet been determined. (Pacific Link)
The court challenge could have implications beyond this project. Roberts Bank Terminal 2 has also been listed for consideration under the Building Canada Act, while Bill C-39, currently before Parliament, would make the national interest designation process permanent and allow entire regions to be designated.
Cold Lake First Nation has also filed its own application for judicial review challenging the Pacific Link designation.
Tsartlip says the pipeline could still move forward through the usual regulatory process. Its challenge is focused on whether the federal government followed its legal obligations before making the national interest designation.
CTV News has reached out to Pacific Link, Trans Mountain Corporation, Pembina Pipeline Corporation and the office of federal Minister Dominic LeBlanc for interviews and comment on the legal challenge. This story will be updated as responses are received.
